Restart techniques are common in gradient-free optimization to deal with multi-
modal functions. Partial warm restarts are also gaining popularity in gradient-
based optimization to improve the rate of convergence in accelerated gradient
schemes to deal with ill-conditioned functions. In this paper, we propose a sim-

The role of implicit regularization.
While explicit regularizers like dropout and weight-decay
may not be essential for generalization, it is certainly the case that not all models that ﬁt the training
data well generalize well. Indeed, in neural networks, we almost always choose our model as the
output of running stochastic gradient descent. Appealing to linear models, we analyze how SGD
acts as an implicit regularizer. For linear models, SGD always converges to a solution with small
norm. Hence, the algorithm itself is implicitly regularizing the solution. Indeed, we show on small
data sets that even Gaussian kernel methods can generalize well with no regularization. Though this
doesn’t explain why certain architectures generalize better than other architectures, it does suggest
that more investigation is needed to understand exactly what the properties are inherited by models
that were trained using SGD.

## Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)

**What it is.** Stochastic gradient descent is the workhorse optimization algorithm for training deep neural networks. It minimizes a loss $\ell(x,\Theta)$ averaged over the training set by taking iterative parameter steps. Rather than computing the true gradient over the whole dataset, at each step it draws a **mini-batch** $x_{1\ldots m}$ of size $m$ and uses it to approximate the gradient, updating parameters against that estimate with learning rate $\alpha$: $\Theta \leftarrow \Theta - \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\partial \ell(x_i,\Theta)}{\partial \Theta}$. Mini-batching helps two ways — the batch gradient is an estimate of the full-training-set gradient whose quality improves with batch size, and batch computation is far more efficient than $m$ single-example steps thanks to hardware parallelism. Its main practical cost is that it "requires careful tuning of the model hyper-parameters, specifically the learning rate ... as well as the initial values for the model parameters." (*Batch Normalization*, Ioffe & Szegedy, 1502.03167, pp. 1, 4). A cleaner one-line form of the update also appears as $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta_t e_t x_{i_t}$, with step size $\eta_t$ and prediction-error $e_t$ (*Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization*, 1611.03530, p. 9).

The corpus treats SGD along several distinct threads:

**1. As the standard training method, plus its variants.** SGD "has proved to be an effective way of training deep networks," with variants such as **momentum** (Sutskever et al., 2013) and **Adagrad** (Duchi et al., 2011) used to reach state-of-the-art performance. Batch-normalized models are trained with "a version of Stochastic Gradient Descent with momentum ... using [a] mini-batch size of 32" (1502.03167, pp. 1, 6). The lottery-ticket experiments likewise use "SGD with momentum (0.9) at various learning rates" (*The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis*, 1803.03635, pp. 25–26). The online/streaming form — "standard online gradient descent (Zinkevich, 2003), which moves the current estimate $\theta_t$ ... in the opposite direction of the [gradient]" — is the baseline against which adaptive optimizers are compared (*Practical Bayesian Neural Networks via Adaptive Optimization Methods*, 1811.03679, p. 1).

**2. As an implicit regularizer / a lens on generalization.** A central modern question is *which* solution SGD selects. "In neural networks, we almost always choose our model as the output of running stochastic gradient descent ... For linear models, SGD always converges to a solution with small norm. Hence, the algorithm itself is implicitly regularizing the solution." The same paper shows SGD "with unchanged hyperparameter settings can optimize the weights to fit ... random labels perfectly," which is why understanding generalization requires inspecting SGD's inductive bias rather than relying on explicit regularizers (1611.03530, pp. 3, 4, 9). Related references in the corpus study SGD's stability ("Train faster, generalize better: Stability of stochastic gradient descent," Hardt et al., ICML 2016, cited on 1611.03530 p. 10) and a Bayesian view of it (Smith & Le, "A Bayesian Perspective on Generalization and Stochastic Gradient Descent," cited in 1712.00409, p. 15).

**3. Improving SGD's convergence — warm restarts.** SGDR proposes "a simple warm restart technique for stochastic gradient descent to improve its anytime performance when training deep neural networks," reporting state-of-the-art CIFAR-10/100 errors of 3.14% and 16.21%. It works by periodically increasing the learning rate to restart optimization, and notes that with SGD's batch-to-batch noise "one should denoise the incoming information ... by considering averaged gradients and losses, e.g., once per epoch" (*SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Restarts*, Loshchilov & Hutter, 1608.03983, pp. 1, 3–4, 12).

**4. As an experimental variable.** Papers vary the optimizer to probe learning behavior. The grokking study contrasts "full-batch gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, large or small learning rates" as regularization interventions (*Grokking*, 2201.02177, p. 3). The lottery-ticket work finds SGD-trained unpruned Conv-2/Conv-4/Conv-6 networks "typically 2-3 percentage points less accurate" than Adam-trained ones, with gradients exploding at high learning rates (1803.03635, p. 31). SGD is also used straightforwardly as the optimizer in scaling-law LSTM/RHN experiments (*Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable*, 1712.00409, p. 7).

**Corpus-level note.** SGD appears in at least 8 of the 100 documents. In two of them it surfaces only as a bibliography entry — the "learning to learn by gradient descent by gradient descent" reference in GPT-3 (2005.14165, p. 68) and the SGDR/Bayesian-SGD citations in 1712.00409 (p. 15) — so those are pointers rather than substantive treatments.
